title: Green wins a wet Hockenheim Race 2 despite a penalty
dek: Jamie Green won Sunday’s race at Hockenheim for Audi by 4.936 seconds from Paffett, overcoming a five-second penalty, as rain and a safety-car restart scrambled the order and Wittmann climbed from 17th to third.

chapters.title: Sunday brings rain and a second restart test
text: Saturday’s opener had gone to Lucas Auer, who won from pole ahead of Timo Glock and Mike Rockenfeller and left the first race at the top of the drivers’ standings. Sunday’s forecast was colder and wetter, with rain threatening a race that needed no more variables: the new tyres had already shown how quickly they could fall away, and the new Indy-style safety-car restart, with the field lined up in two rows, had still not been used in a race.

chapters.title: Glock gambles on slicks and takes pole
text: The session ran on a damp, drying track. Everyone started on wet tyres, and Edoardo Mortara set the early benchmark before the cars came back in. Glock was the first to try slicks, around the halfway point of the 20 minutes, and immediately jumped up the order, then drifted down it as others followed and the track kept improving. He saved his best for the last minute: 1:31.406 for the second pole of his DTM career and three championship points.

René Rast took the other front-row slot, 0.175 seconds behind, for Audi Team Rosberg, and his team-mate Jamie Green was third at 0.233. Mortara was fourth, Rockenfeller fifth and Bruno Spengler sixth, with Gary Paffett seventh and Saturday’s winner Auer eighth, 0.662 seconds off. Maro Engel was ninth and Mattias Ekström tenth, having won a World Rallycross round that morning before climbing into his DTM car.

The big casualty was Augusto Farfus. His final lap would have put him second, but he crossed the line a fraction of a second after the session had ended, his time was deleted, and he dropped to 18th and last. Marco Wittmann, the champion, was 17th.

chapters.title: A first-corner crash, then a chaotic Indy restart
text: Glock led away from pole, but at the back of the field the first corner went wrong. Robert Wickens tried to dive up the inside of Nico Müller and the two collided, Duval turned in on them, and Wickens ended in the gravel. The safety car was needed to recover his Mercedes, and Rast, who had bogged down off the line, lost places in the opening moments.

The restart was the first Indy-style one of the season, with the cars side by side in two rows, and it went badly for Glock. He lost three places in a few hundred metres to Green, Auer and Spengler, who passed him as the lights went out. Behind them, Rast and Maxime Martin collided at once, and Martin later said the contact broke his suspension; both were out within four laps. Duval parked later, after the damage from the start.
Green was handed a five-second penalty for starting his move too early, to be served at his pit stop, but he built a gap fast enough to cover it.

chapters.title: Slicks, wets and a late stop for Wittmann
text: Around half distance the rain arrived, and the compulsory stops became a lottery. Glock and Spengler had already stopped for slicks before the rain strengthened and had to come in again, and Glock later admitted he had gambled that the shower would be short. Rockenfeller also stopped early on slicks and then swapped to wets.

The winners were those who waited. Wittmann, who had been carried forward from 17th on the grid by the restart, delayed his mandatory stop until he could take wet tyres directly and rose into the podium positions. Paffett stopped with the pack once the rain was heavy. Auer, on slicks, radioed that he needed wets, pitted, and rejoined behind Wittmann and Paffett after running wide at the hairpin on his out-lap.
Green stopped a lap later than most of those who had waited, still served his five seconds, and regained the lead when Auer came in two laps afterwards.

chapters.title: Green holds off Paffett
text: From there Green managed the gap. He won after 32 laps in 56m53.264s, 4.936 seconds clear of Paffett, who had passed Wittmann at the hairpin for second and held it. Wittmann finished third, 8.191 seconds behind, with Auer fourth, 16.985 seconds back. It was Green’s first win since Zandvoort in 2016, and his 1:33.614 on lap seven was the fastest lap of the race.

Müller held off Paul di Resta for fifth by less than half a second, with Rockenfeller seventh. Glock recovered to eighth, ahead of Spengler and Engel, with Ekström 11th and Mortara a lap down in 13th. Wickens, Rast, Martin, Duval and Farfus were the five retirements. Again all three manufacturers stood on the podium: Audi, Mercedes and BMW.

chapters.title: A warning for Green, a lead for Auer
text: Green’s win was not secured until well after the flag. He stopped on the start-finish straight to celebrate with his mechanics, and race direction investigated both that and the restart. The result stood, with a warning for stopping on the straight. Green said he had been following the race director’s “green” call, and that he had simply tried to keep pace with Glock. Glock thought differently: he believed Green had not stuck to the rules at the restart, and said he did not understand the five-second penalty.

Mercedes had its own reason to be pleased. Ulrich Fritz called Paffett’s drive sensational after his early setbacks, and Paffett’s second place followed Auer’s win and fourth place. Auer left Hockenheim leading the drivers’ standings on 40 points, with Green and Paffett tied for second on 26.

For BMW it was a weekend of contrasts. Wittmann called his third place, from 17th on the grid, “a mega race” and said it felt like a victory, and BMW Motorsport Director Jens Marquardt praised the fight back. Team principal Stefan Reinhold said the new M4 ran superbly in the rain, and admitted Glock’s stop had been too early after the team expected slicks to last. BMW also took two retirements, with Martin and Farfus both failing to finish.
Audi had won with Green, but lost Rast and Duval to retirements. The next round is at the Lausitzring, on 20–21 May.

facts.v: Rain began to fall around half distance, forcing most of the field to switch to wet tyres, and Wittmann delayed his stop to go straight onto wets.
